claim: Cellulosomal cohesin-dockerin (Coh-Doc) pairs are believed to interact through redundant dual binding modes consisting of two distinct conformations.
source: Receptor-ligand pairs are ordinarily thought to interact through a lock and key mechanism, where a unique molecular conformation is formed upon binding. Contrary to this paradigm, cellulosomal cohesin-dockerin (Coh-Doc) pairs are believed to interact through redundant dual binding modes consisting of two distinct conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior literature and established understanding in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'are believed to'.

claim: Single-molecule force spectroscopy (SMFS) was used to discriminate two binding modes of Coh:Doc complexes based on distinct differences in their mechanical properties.
source: Although average bulk measurements were unable to resolve the differences in Doc binding modes due to the similarity of the interactions, with a single-molecule method we were able to discriminate the two modes based on distinct differences in their mechanical properties.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results from SMFS measurements showing distinct mechanical properties for different binding modes.

claim: Wild-type Doc from Clostridium thermocellum exocellulase Cel48S populates both binding modes with similar probabilities under native conditions.
source: We conclude that under native conditions wild-type Doc from Clostridium thermocellum exocellulase Cel48S populates both binding modes with similar probabilities.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly the single-molecule measurements.

claim: Cellulosomes are hierarchically branching protein networks developed by nature for efficient deconstruction of lignocellulosic biomass.
source: Cellulosomes are hierarchically branching protein networks developed by nature for efficient deconstruction of lignocellulosic biomass.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on cellulosomes.

claim: Cellulosomes incorporate catalytic domains, carbohydrate binding modules (CBMs), cohesin:dockerin (Coh:Doc) pairs, and other conserved features.
source: These enzyme complexes incorporate catalytic domains, carbohydrate binding modules (CBMs), cohesin:dockerin (Coh:Doc) pairs, and other conserved features (Demain et al., 2005; Bayer et al., 2004; Schwarz, 2001; Béguin and Aubert, 1994; Smith and Bayer, 2013; Fontes and Gilbert, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple literature citations.

claim: The type-I Doc domain is typically found at the C-terminus of cellulosomal catalytic domains and is approximately 75 amino acids in length.
source: A central attribute of cellulosome assembly is the conserved ~75 amino acid type-I Doc domain typically found at the C-terminus of cellulosomal catalytic domains.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellulosome structure.

claim: Dockerins guide attachment of enzymes into cellulosome networks by binding strongly to conserved Coh domains organized within non-catalytic poly (Coh) scaffolds.
source: Dockerins guide attachment of enzymes into the networks by binding strongly to conserved Coh domains organized within non-catalytic poly (Coh) scaffolds.
evidence: This describes the functional role of dockerins based on established knowledge.

claim: Many archetypal Coh:Doc pairs exhibit nanomolar binding affinities.
source: In addition to their nanomolar binding affinities, many archetypal Coh:Doc pairs are thought to exhibit dual binding modes (Carvalho et al., 2007; Pinheiro et al., 2008; Currie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Many archetypal Coh:Doc pairs are thought to exhibit dual binding modes.
source: In addition to their nanomolar binding affinities, many archetypal Coh:Doc pairs are thought to exhibit dual binding modes (Carvalho et al., 2007; Pinheiro et al., 2008; Currie et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The two binding modes of Doc differ by approximately 180° rotation on the Coh surface.
source: The bound Doc domain can adopt two possible orientations that differ by ~180° rotation on the Coh surface, as shown in Figure 1B.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1B and referenced literature.

claim: The two binding modes originate from duplicated F-hand sequence motifs found among type-I dockerins.
source: The two binding modes originate from duplicated F-hand sequence motifs, a conserved structural feature found among type-I dockerins (Pagès et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The duplicated F-hand motifs in dockerins resemble EF-hands found in eukaryotic calcium binding proteins such as calmodulin.
source: The duplicated F-hand motifs resemble EF-hands found in eukaryotic calcium binding proteins (e.g., calmodulin), and provide internal sequence and structural symmetry to Doc domains.
evidence: This is based on structural similarity and established knowledge.

claim: Rotating Doc by approximately 180° with respect to Coh results in an alternatively bound complex with similarly high affinity involving the same residues on Coh recognizing mirrored residues within Doc.
source: Rotating Doc by ~180° with respect to Coh (Figure 1B,C) results in an alternatively bound complex with similarly high affinity involving the same residues on Coh recognizing mirrored residues within Doc.
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The dual binding mode is thought to increase the conformational space available to densely packed enzymes on protein scaffolds.
source: The dual binding mode is thought to increase the conformational space available to densely packed enzymes on protein scaffolds, and to facilitate substrate recognition by catalytic domains within cellulosomal networks (Bayer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The dual binding mode facilitates substrate recognition by catalytic domains within cellulosomal networks.
source: The dual binding mode is thought to increase the conformational space available to densely packed enzymes on protein scaffolds, and to facilitate substrate recognition by catalytic domains within cellulosomal networks (Bayer et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The dual binding mode confers robustness against loss-of-function mutations from an evolutionary perspective.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, the dual binding mode confers robustness against loss-of-function mutations, while allowing mutations within Doc to explore inter-bacterial species cohesin-binding promiscuity in cellulosome-producing microbial communities.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary advantages based on the structural properties.

claim: The dual binding mode allows mutations within Doc to explore inter-bacterial species cohesin-binding promiscuity in cellulosome-producing microbial communities.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, the dual binding mode confers robustness against loss-of-function mutations, while allowing mutations within Doc to explore inter-bacterial species cohesin-binding promiscuity in cellulosome-producing microbial communities.
evidence: This is an inference about evolutionary advantages based on the structural properties.

claim: Direct experimental observation of the dual binding modes for wild-type Doc has proven challenging.
source: However, direct experimental observation of the dual binding modes for wild-type Doc has thus far proven challenging.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation in the field.

claim: Ensemble average bulk biochemical assays are of limited use in resolving binding mode populations when the binding modes are of equal thermodynamic affinity.
source: Ensemble average bulk biochemical assays (e.g., surface plasmon resonance, calorimetry, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays) are of limited use in resolving binding mode populations, particularly when the binding modes are of equal thermodynamic affinity.
evidence: This is based on the inherent limitations of ensemble methods.

claim: Crystallography of Coh:Doc complexes is challenging because the complex does not adopt a unique molecular conformation but exhibits a mixture of two conformations, hindering crystal growth.
source: Crystallography is challenging because the complex does not adopt a unique molecular conformation, but rather exhibits a mixture of two conformations thereby hindering crystal growth.
evidence: This explains a technical challenge based on the nature of the dual binding mode.

claim: Structural data on the dual binding mode have typically been collected using a mutagenesis approach where one of the binding modes was destabilized by mutating key recognition elements.
source: Structural data on the dual binding mode have typically been collected using a mutagenesis approach, where one of the binding modes was destabilized by mutating key recognition elements (Carvalho et al., 2007; Pinheiro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing this methodology.

claim: The mutagenesis approach for obtaining structural data cannot determine if one binding mode is dominant for wild-type Doc or if that dominance is species or sequence dependent.
source: This approach, however, while resolving the structures of each bound complex, cannot determine if one binding mode is dominant for wild-type Doc, or if that dominance is species or sequence dependent.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of the mutagenesis approach.

claim: Coarse grained molecular dynamics has predicted dual modes of interaction between Coh and Doc.
source: Coarse grained molecular dynamics has also predicted dual modes of interaction between Coh and Doc (Hall and Sansom, 2009), but direct experimental evidence of both binding modes for wild-type Doc has remained elusive.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior computational work.

claim: Direct experimental evidence of both binding modes for wild-type Doc has remained elusive.
source: Coarse grained molecular dynamics has also predicted dual modes of interaction between Coh and Doc (Hall and Sansom, 2009), but direct experimental evidence of both binding modes for wild-type Doc has remained elusive.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the existing literature.

claim: Doc mutants Q1 and Q3 were designed to exhibit a preferred binding mode.
source: To validate our approach, we produced Doc mutants that exhibited a preferred binding mode.
evidence: This describes the experimental design approach used in the study.

claim: Single-molecule pulling experiments on bound Coh:mutant Doc complexes observed a strong bias in the probability of two clearly distinguishable unfolding patterns termed 'single' and 'double' rupture types for each binding mode mutant.
source: We performed single-molecule pulling experiments on bound Coh:mutant Doc complexes and observed a strong bias in the probability of two clearly distinguishable unfolding patterns, termed 'single' and 'double' rupture types for each binding mode mutant.
evidence: This describes experimental observations from SMFS measurements.

claim: Poly (Gly-Ser) inserts were used to add amino acid sequence length to specific sections of Doc to identify which portions of Doc unfolded.
source: We further probed the unbinding mechanism of the double rupture events using poly (Gly-Ser) inserts to add amino acid sequence length to specific sections of Doc as a means to identify which portions of Doc unfolded.
evidence: This describes an experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The inherent differences in mechanical stability of each binding mode were used to directly observe and quantify binding mode populations for wild-type Doc.
source: Finally, we used the inherent differences in mechanical stability of each binding mode, and the effects these differences had on the unfolding force distributions of an adjacent domain, to directly observe and quantify binding mode populations for wild-type Doc.
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used to quantify binding modes.

claim: A Ser-Thr pair located at positions 11 and 12 of F-hand motif 1 (N-terminal helix 1) is highly conserved among Ct-Doc domains.
source: Among Ct-Doc domains, a Ser-Thr pair located at positions 11 and 12 of F-hand motif 1 (N-terminal helix 1) is highly conserved (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The Ser-Thr pair at positions 11 and 12 is H-bonded to Coh in binding mode A.
source: This Ser-Thr pair is H-bonded to Coh in binding mode A (Figure 1A, black dots).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Binding mode B refers to the configuration where the Ser-Thr pair from helix 3 dominates the H-bonding to Coh.
source: Analogously, binding mode B refers to the configuration where the Ser-Thr pair from helix 3 dominates the H-bonding to Coh (Figure 1A, gray dots).
evidence: This is supported by structural data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Binding mode B was previously crystallized for a homologous Ct-Doc.
source: Binding mode B was previously crystallized for a homologous Ct-Doc (Carvalho et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mutation of the Ser-Thr pair in helix 3 to Ala-Ala was used to bias binding and thereby crystallize binding mode A for a Ct-Doc.
source: Mutation of the Ser-Thr pair in helix 3 to Ala-Ala was used to bias binding and thereby crystallize binding mode A for the same Doc (Carvalho et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A similar targeted mutagenesis approach was used to obtain crystal structures of a Clostridium cellulolyticum Doc in each binding mode.
source: A similar targeted mutagenesis approach was also used to obtain crystal structures of a Clostridium cellulolyticum Doc in each binding mode (Pinheiro et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Quadruple mutants (Q1 and Q3) were designed to preferentially select for a specific binding mode (A or B).
source: To preferentially select for a specific binding mode (A or B), we prepared Doc sequences that incorporated 4 amino acid point mutations, referred to as quadruple mutants ('Q').
evidence: This describes the experimental design approach.

claim: Non-canonical Ct-Doc domains that differ from the canonical duplicated Ser-Thr sequences were found to exhibit only a single binding mode.
source: To design quadruple mutants, we noted that recent structural work reported a set of Ct-Doc domains that differ from the canonical duplicated Ser-Thr sequences. These non-canonical Docs were found to exhibit only a single binding mode (Brás et al., 2012; Pinheiro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In one non-canonical Doc domain, an Asp-Glu pair was found in place of Ser-Thr.
source: In one of these non-canonical Doc domains, an Asp-Glu pair was found in place of Ser-Thr.
evidence: This is based on structural information from prior literature.

claim: Including Asp-Glu in place of Ser-Thr within one of the F-hands could be used to effectively knock out a given binding mode because the Coh surface is negatively charged.
source: Since the Coh surface is negatively charged, we postulated that including Asp-Glu in place of Ser-Thr within one of the F-hands could be used to effectively knock out a given binding mode for our canonical Doc.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on electrostatic considerations.

claim: Double alanine mutations were incorporated to replace the conserved Lys-18 Arg-19 residues of a given F-hand motif to further destabilize a targeted binding mode.
source: Additionally, we incorporated double alanine mutations to replace the conserved Lys-18 Arg-19 residues of a given F-hand motif, further destabilizing a targeted binding mode.
evidence: This describes the experimental design approach.

claim: Q1 refers to a quadruple mutant where helix 1 has been modified at four positions (S11D-T12E-K18A-R19A).
source: Q1 refers to a quadruple mutant where helix 1 has been modified at four positions (i.e. S11D-T12E-K18A-R19A).
evidence: This describes the specific mutations made in the Q1 mutant.

claim: Q3 refers to the quadruple mutant where helix 3 has been modified at four positions (S43D-T44E-K50A-R51A).
source: Q3 refers to the quadruple mutant where helix 3 has been modified at four positions (i.e. S43D-T44E-K50A-R51A).
evidence: This describes the specific mutations made in the Q3 mutant.

claim: QQ mutant incorporated quadruple mutations into both helices 1 and 3 and served as a negative control.
source: As a negative control, we prepared a mutant referred to as 'QQ' that incorporated quadruple mutations into both helices 1 and 3.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the negative control.

claim: Doc domains were expressed as fusion domains attached to the C-terminal end of xylanaseT6 from Geobacillus stearothermophilus to improve solubility and expression levels.
source: Doc domains were expressed as fusion domains attached to the C-terminal end of xylanaseT6 (Xyn) from Geobacillus stearothermophilus to improve solubility and expression levels as previously reported (Stahl et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach and is supported by a citation.

claim: The Xyn domain acts as a fingerprint in AFM force extension traces to provide a means for screening datasets and searching for known contour length increments.
source: The Xyn domain also acts as a so-called fingerprint in AFM force extension traces to provide a means for screening datasets and searching for known contour length increments.
evidence: This describes the methodological role of the Xyn domain.

claim: Cohesin 2 from Ct-CipA was expressed as a C-terminal fusion domain with the family 3a carbohydrate binding module (CBM) from Ct-CipA.
source: For the Coh domain, we chose cohesin 2 from Ct-CipA expressed as a C-terminal fusion domain with the family 3a carbohydrate binding module (CBM) from Ct-CipA.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the Coh construct.

claim: A second set of fusion proteins was cloned, expressed and probed in complementary experiments using a flavoprotein domain from the plant blue light receptor phototropin (iLOV) to exclude artifacts arising from fingerprint domains, protein immobilization or pulling geometry.
source: In order to exclude artifacts arising from fingerprint domains, protein immobilization or pulling geometry, a second set of fusion proteins was cloned, expressed and probed in complementary experiments using a flavoprotein domain from the plant blue light receptor phototropin (iLOV) (Chapman et al., 2008).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for control experiments and is supported by a citation.

claim: CBM-Coh was site-specifically and covalently attached to an AFM cantilever tip.
source: CBM-Coh was site-specifically and covalently attached to an AFM cantilever tip and brought into contact with a glass surface modified with Xyn-Doc.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup for AFM measurements.

claim: The mechanical strength of protein domains and complexes strongly depends on the pulling points (sites at which the molecule is attached to cantilever/surface).
source: The mechanical strength of protein domains and complexes will strongly depend on the pulling points (i.e. sites at which the molecule is attached to cantilever/surface).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of single-molecule force spectroscopy.

claim: The site-specific attachment chemistry ensured the same loading geometry was used on the complex for each and every data trace.
source: The site-specific attachment chemistry used here was precisely defined by the chosen residue of immobilization, ensuring the same loading geometry was used on the complex for each and every data trace.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to ensure reproducibility.

claim: The cantilever retraction speed ranged from 200 to 3200 nm/s during AFM measurements.
source: After formation of the Coh:Doc complex, the cantilever was retracted at a constant speed that ranged from 200 to 3200 nm/s while the force was monitored by optical cantilever deflection.
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters used in AFM measurements.

claim: A sawtooth pattern was consistently observed in force-distance traces when molecular ligand-receptor complexes had formed.
source: A sawtooth pattern was consistently observed when molecular ligand-receptor complexes had formed.
evidence: This describes the characteristic signature of single-molecule interactions in AFM.

claim: Contour length transformation and identification of traces containing a Xyn contour length increment (~89 nm) allowed screening for single-molecule interactions.
source: Sorting the data using contour length transformation (Puchner et al., 2008) and identifying traces that contained a Xyn contour length increment (~89 nm) allowed us to screen for single-molecule interactions (Stahl et al., 2012), as described in our prior work on Coh:Doc dissociation under force (Stahl et al., 2012; Schoeler et al., 2014; Jobst et al., 2013; Otten et al., 2014; Schoeler et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methodology and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Coh:Doc complex rupture occurred in two distinct event types: single and double ruptures.
source: The Coh:Doc complex rupture occurred in two distinct event types: single (B) and double (C) ruptures.
evidence: This is supported by the force-extension traces shown in Figures 3B and 3C.

claim: The 8-nm contour length increment separating the double peaks was assigned to Doc unfolding.
source: The 8-nm contour length increment separating the double peaks was assigned to Doc unfolding (C, green).
evidence: This is an assignment based on the experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The 8-nm contour length increment was also observed in complementary experiments employing other fusion domains where xylanase was swapped for an sfGFP domain and CBM was swapped out for an iLOV domain.
source: The 8-nm contour length increment was also observed in complementary experiments employing other fusion domains: xylanase was swapped for an sfGFP domain and CBM was swapped out for an iLOV domain. In these new fusions, the 8 nm Doc increment was still observed, indicating it was not caused by a specific fusion domain.
evidence: This describes control experiments that validate the assignment of the 8-nm increment to Doc.

claim: Double and single rupture events were associated with binding modes A and B, respectively.
source: As we show below, double and single rupture events were associated with binding modes A and B, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented later in the manuscript.

claim: CBM unfolding length increments (~57 nm) were only rarely observed because the Coh:Doc complex only rarely withstood forces sufficiently high to unfold CBM.
source: CBM unfolding length increments (~57 nm) were only rarely observed because the Coh:Doc complex only rarely withstood forces sufficiently high to unfold CBM (Stahl et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data and is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Q1 and Q3 Doc sequences maintained high-binding affinity with dissociation constants (Kd) in the nM range.
source: The data clearly showed that Q1 and Q3 Doc sequences, each with a mutated binding mode, maintained high-binding affinity with dissociation constants (Kd) in the nM range.
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The dissociation constants for Q1 and Q3 mutants are in good agreement with previous reports on homologous type-I Doc domains.
source: These values are in good agreement with previous reports on homologous type-I Doc domains (Brás et al., 2012; Sakka et al., 2011).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutant Doc domains with one destabilized binding mode were still able to recognize fluorescent protein fused Coh with strong affinity by relying on the alternative binding mode that was preserved.
source: This suggested that mutant Doc domains with one destabilized binding mode were still able to recognize fluorescent protein fused Coh with strong affinity by relying on the alternative binding mode that was preserved.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the binding data.

claim: The QQ double knockout mutant showed no appreciable binding over the concentration range tested.
source: The QQ double knockout mutant, however, showed no appreciable binding over the concentration range tested.
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DEAA quadruple mutations were effective at eliminating binding for the targeted modes.
source: This negative control showed that DEAA quadruple mutations were in fact effective at eliminating binding for the targeted modes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the QQ mutant binding data.

claim: Wild-type Doc showed double rupture events in approximately 57% of the cases and single rupture events in approximately 43% of the cases.
source: The wild-type Doc showed double rupture events in ~57% of the cases, and single rupture events in ~43% of the cases.
evidence: This is supported by the event probability data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Q1 mutant showed a single event probability of approximately 77% and a double event probability of approximately 23%.
source: The mutant designed to knock out binding mode A (Q1), showed a single event probability of ~77%, and a double event probability of ~23%.
evidence: This is supported by the event probability data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Q3 mutant showed a single event probability of approximately 41% and a double event probability of approximately 59%.
source: The mutant designed to knock out binding mode B (Q3) showed a single event probability of ~41%, and a double event probability of ~59%.
evidence: This is supported by the event probability data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The Q1 mutant has a strong bias toward single peaks that is not observed in the wild-type, leading to preliminary assignment of single peaks to binding mode B.
source: It is clear from these data that the Q1 mutant has a strong bias toward single peaks that is not observed in the wild-type leading to preliminary assignment of single peaks to binding mode B.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the event probability data.

claim: Q1 and wild-type on average showed second peaks that were approximately 15-20% higher in force than the first peak for double events.
source: Q1 and wild-type on average showed second peaks that were ~15–20% higher in force than the first peak.
evidence: This is supported by the force difference data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Double peaks for the Q3 mutant were more likely to show a shielded behavior where the second peak was lower in force than the first peak by approximately 10%.
source: Double peaks for the Q3 mutant were more likely to show a shielded behavior, where the second peak was lower in force than the first peak by ~10%.
evidence: This is supported by the force difference data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The second barrier of the double events was weaker in Q3 than for wild-type.
source: The second barrier of the double events was therefore weaker in Q3 than for wild-type.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the force difference data.

claim: The number of double peaks is being underestimated systematically for the Q3 mutant due to the weaker 2nd double peak combined with similar single/double peak ratios as wild-type.
source: This weaker 2nd double peak for the Q3 mutant combined with similar single/double peak ratios as wild-type leads us to believe that the number of double peaks is being underestimated systematically for the Q3 mutant.
evidence: This is an inference about systematic bias in the measurements.

claim: Each binding mode allows for the occurrence of a single event (albeit with different likelihood) in which the whole Doc domain unbinds without an additional unfolding substep.
source: Generally, each binding mode still allows for the occurrence of a single event (albeit with different likelihood), in which the whole Doc domain unbinds without an additional unfolding substep.
evidence: This is an inference about the unbinding mechanism.

claim: Since the second and final energy barrier for complex dissociation is weaker than the first for the Q3 mutant, the probability for the molecule to pass both barriers simultaneously is increased, resulting in a higher percentage of single events.
source: Since the second and final energy barrier for complex dissociation is weaker than the first for the Q3 mutant, the probability for the molecule to pass both barriers simultaneously is increased, thus resulting in a higher percentage of single events.
evidence: This is an inference about the energy landscape and its effect on observed events.

claim: A (Gly-Ser)8 linker was incorporated between helix 1 and helix 2 in a flexible loop that was not expected to interfere with either of the two binding modes.
source: In this case, we engineered flexible (GS)8 insert sequences directly into wild-type Doc between helices 1 and 2, in a flexible loop that was not expected to interfere with either of the two binding modes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the GS-insert mutant.

claim: The contour length histogram for (GS)8 Doc was indistinguishable from the wild-type Doc.
source: As shown in Figure 5B,C and D, the contour length histogram for (GS)8 Doc was indistinguishable from the wild-type Doc.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5.

claim: No additional contour length was gained due to additional amino acids inserted between Doc helices 1 and 2.
source: No additional contour length was gained due to additional amino acids inserted between Doc helices 1 and 2.
evidence: This is an observation from the GS-insert experiment data.

claim: The unfolding event responsible for the 8-nm length increment must be located upstream (N-terminal) from the site of the (GS)8-insert.
source: Since the Doc was anchored to the glass slide through an N-terminal xylanase domain, this result indicated that the unfolding event responsible for the 8-nm length increment must be located upstream (i.e. N-terminal) from the site of the (GS)8-insert.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GS-insert experiment results.

claim: Unfolding of calcium binding loop 1 and helix 1 in Doc was the source of the 8-nm length increment.
source: This result suggested that unfolding of calcium binding loop 1 and helix 1 in Doc was the source of the 8-nm length increment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GS-insert experiment results.

claim: The most probable rupture force for single events was approximately 104 pN at a pulling speed of 800 nm/s.
source: The most probable rupture force for single events was ~104 pN, while for double events this value was ~140 pN at a pulling speed of 800 nm/s.
evidence: This is supported by the rupture force distribution data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The most probable rupture force for double events (second peak) was approximately 140 pN at a pulling speed of 800 nm/s.
source: The most probable rupture force for single events was ~104 pN, while for double events this value was ~140 pN at a pulling speed of 800 nm/s.
evidence: This is supported by the rupture force distribution data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Each binding mode has a distinct mechanical stability and energy landscape that is set at the time of receptor-ligand binding.
source: Each mode has a distinct mechanical stability and energy landscape that is set at the time of receptor-ligand binding, that is once bound, the conformation of the complex does not change.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the binding mode affects the iLOV unfolding force distribution.

claim: Once bound, the conformation of the Coh:Doc complex does not change.
source: Each mode has a distinct mechanical stability and energy landscape that is set at the time of receptor-ligand binding, that is once bound, the conformation of the complex does not change.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the binding mode affects the iLOV unfolding force distribution.

claim: If single- and double-event unbinding patterns were simply two competing pathways out of the same bound state, then the downward shift in rupture force distribution would not be observed for the iLOV unfolding forces.
source: If single- and double-event unbinding patterns were simply two competing pathways out of the same bound state, then the downward shift in rupture force distribution would not be observed for the iLOV unfolding forces.
evidence: This is a logical argument supporting the interpretation of the data.

claim: The datasets for both binding modes were measured with the same cantilever throughout the runtime of the whole experiment.
source: We note that the datasets for both binding modes were measured with the same cantilever throughout the runtime of the whole experiment.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure to ensure data quality.

claim: Calibration and drift issues did not interfere with the required accuracy of the measurements.
source: Calibration and drift issues therefore did not interfere with the required accuracy.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality control of the measurements.

claim: The first barrier of the double peaks represents unfolding of the N-terminal calcium binding loop and unraveling of alpha helix 1 up to the Lys-Arg pair at sequence positions 18 and 19 in the wild-type structure in binding mode A.
source: Taken together, we propose an unbinding mechanism where the first barrier of the double peaks represents unfolding of the N-terminal calcium binding loop and unraveling of alpha helix 1 up to the Lys-Arg pair at sequence positions 18 and 19 in the wild-type structure in binding mode A.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and structural information.

claim: Based on a length per stretched amino acid of 0.4 nm, the expected contour length for unfolding the Doc domain up to position 18-19 would be 7.6 nm, in good agreement with the measured value of 8 nm.
source: Based on a length per stretched amino acid of 0.4 nm, the expected contour length for unfolding the Doc domain up to this position would be 7.6 nm, in good agreement with the measured value of 8 nm within experimental error.
evidence: This is a calculation based on structural information that supports the proposed mechanism.

claim: A portion of the N-terminal calcium binding loop (residues S11-T12) is involved in binding to D39 in Coh.
source: A portion of the N-terminal calcium binding loop (i.e. residues S11-T12) is involved in binding to D39 in Coh.
evidence: This is based on structural information from crystal structures.

claim: The first peak of the double events is attributed to breakage of the S11-T12 interaction with Coh and simultaneous unfolding of calcium loop 1 and alpha helix 1 up to the Lys-Arg pair at sequence positions 18 and 19.
source: The first peak of the double events is attributed to breakage of this interaction and simultaneous unfolding of calcium loop 1 and alpha helix 1 up to the Lys-Arg pair at sequence positions 18 and 19.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental data and structural information.

claim: An intramolecular clasp has been identified as a stabilizing mechanism among similar type-I Doc domains.
source: Another contributing factor is the intramolecular clasp that has been identified as a stabilizing mechanism among similar type-I Doc domains (Slutzki et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A recent NMR structural study on the same wild-type Doc used in this work confirmed a hydrophobic ring-stacking interaction between Tyr-5 and Pro-66.
source: A recent NMR structural study (Chen et al., 2014) on the same wild-type Doc used in this work confirmed a hydrophobic ring-stacking interaction between Tyr-5 and Pro-66.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Confirmation of the clasp motif by NMR means the head and tail of the Doc are bound together, additionally stabilizing the barrier that is overcome in the first of the double event peaks.
source: Confirmation of this clasp motif by NMR means the head and tail of the Doc are bound together, additionally stabilizing the barrier that is overcome in the first of the double event peaks.
